verdicts.quote: An optometrist may not: (a) perform surgery, including laser surgery
verdicts.reasoning: The statute explicitly prohibits optometrists from performing laser surgery. No laser procedures are authorized.

verdicts.quote: removal of a foreign body from the eye or its adnexa, that is not deeper than the anterior 1/2 of the cornea
verdicts.reasoning: The statute explicitly includes foreign body removal (limited to anterior 1/2 of cornea) in the definition of optometry practice. Beyond that, no other minor surgical procedures are explicitly granted. The foreign body removal is already noted as excluded from the field description, and no additional procedures appear in the text.

verdicts.likely_source: administrative rules (division rules) or a separate therapeutic pharmaceutical agents chapter
verdicts.reasoning: The statute broadly authorizes prescribing pharmaceutical agents for the eye and its adnexa and references 'ocular conditions or diseases specified by division rule,' but does not explicitly mention glaucoma treatment. Specific disease authorizations like glaucoma would likely be addressed in division rules.

verdicts.likely_source: administrative rules or a separate emergency treatment statute
verdicts.reasoning: The statute does not mention epinephrine, anaphylaxis, or emergency injection authority. Section 58-16a-302(4) references 'emergency medical care' training but does not grant specific anaphylaxis treatment authority.

verdicts.quote: prescription, ordering, administration, or adaptation of ophthalmic lenses, contact lenses, ophthalmic devices, pharmaceutical agents, laboratory tests, or ocular exercises to diagnose and treat diseases, defects, or other abnormal conditions of the human eye and its adnexa
verdicts.reasoning: The definition of optometry includes 'ocular exercises' which encompasses vision therapy/orthoptics/visual training within the scope of practice.

The statute contains no mention of immunizations or vaccines. The pharmaceutical agent authority is limited to the eye and its adnexa, and no immunization authority is granted or referenced anywhere in the text.

verdicts.likely_source: Utah Controlled Substances Act (Title 58, Chapter 37) or DEA federal regulations
verdicts.reasoning: The statute references Schedule II and III controlled substances and hydrocodone combination drugs but does not mention DEA registration requirements. That requirement would be found in the controlled substances chapter or federal law.

verdicts.quote: The division shall issue to a person who qualifies under this chapter a license in the classification of optometrist.
verdicts.reasoning: The statute establishes only one license classification: optometrist. There are no tiered license types described.
The statute does not establish any specialty certifications beyond basic licensure. No additional scope-unlocking certifications are mentioned.

verdicts.likely_source: administrative rules or division rules implementing Section 58-16a-302(4)
verdicts.reasoning: Section 58-16a-302(4) requires pre-1996 graduates to complete 'a course of study satisfactory to the division...in general and ocular pharmacology and emergency medical care' but specifies no clock hours. Specific hour requirements would be in division rules.
The statute does not require a supervised clinical internship or preceptorship for expanded pharmaceutical authority or any other purpose. No such requirement appears in the text.

The statute does not require co-management with an ophthalmologist for any procedures. Since optometrists cannot perform surgery under this statute, pre/post-operative co-management requirements are not applicable.

verdicts.likely_source: a separate telehealth statute (e.g., Utah Telehealth Act) or division rules
verdicts.reasoning: The statute does not address telemedicine or telehealth delivery of optometric services. This would likely be addressed in a separate telehealth statute or division rules.

The statute does not address mobile optometric offices. Note that exemptions for contact lens sellers require 'a permanently located and established place of business,' but no provision addresses mobile offices for licensed optometrists.
The statute contains no provision requiring a special permit or registration for home visits. No such requirement appears anywhere in the text.
The statute places no limit on the number of offices an optometrist or group may operate. No such restriction appears in the text.

verdicts.likely_source: a separate spectacle prescription release statute or federal FTC Eyeglass Rule
verdicts.reasoning: The statute requires release of contact lens prescriptions (Section 58-16a-306) but does not explicitly require release of spectacle/ophthalmic lens prescriptions to patients. A separate provision or federal rule may govern this.

verdicts.likely_source: Title 58 general provisions (Section 58-1-401 or related sections) or a separate health professional assistance program statute
verdicts.reasoning: The statute does not establish or reference an impaired practitioner program. Such programs are typically found in general occupational licensing provisions or separate statutes.
The statute does not provide for a limited teaching or faculty license. No such provision appears in the text.

verdicts.likely_source: Title 58 general provisions (Section 58-1-308 or related renewal sections) or division rules
verdicts.reasoning: The statute does not mention a retired license status. Such provisions, if they exist, would likely be in the general licensing chapter (Title 58, Chapter 1) or division rules.

verdicts.quote: have passed examinations approved by the division in consultation with the board that include: (a) a standardized national optometry examination; (b) a standardized clinical examination; and (c) a standardized national therapeutics examination
